utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. But before I say any further word, Madam Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. No preliminaries. Nothing special. So just another 30 seconds for reflection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I might, since we have the time, just inquire about what my friend's intention with the associated exhibits are. I noticed they didn't -- they weren't addressed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender those three remaining documents since two out of five are already admitted under P numbers. So we would offer three remaining documents, 1D4271, 1D4272, and Prosecution 65 ter 09827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we wouldn't have any objections. I noticed in the Karadzic case the witness was asked to explain how the map, I believe that's 4272 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- was created, and if Mr. Lukic is agreeable to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll proceed as suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could already sign numbers. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D4271 receives number D692. Document 1D4272 receives number D693. And document 9827 receives number D694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deal with the matter and decide on admission but do that after we have continued -- resumed the examination of the witness. Mr. Ujic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Lukic will now continue his examination-in-chief. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you briefly something about the police. Did the Serbian policemen separate by themselves or was that based on some kind of agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. Since the Serbian police was in minority, they didn't feel safe in the majority police. So literally, at the very beginning they'd move from the station to the western part of the town. Later on during the negotiations, they were allowed access to the same building only from the other side. So the Muslim police occupied the ground floor and the Serbian police had access to the backdoor or the fire escape door to the second floor and this is where they had their premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the uniforms of the Serbian police, was there an inscription SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. They only had a coat of arms and the Serbian three-coloured flag, and they also had a badge on their caps in three colours as well. There were no other insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you're going to give us a rather long answer, but please make an effort to explain to us as briefly as possible whether you were present the gathering following the -- of the mobilisation of the 216th Brigade in Han Pijesak in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat the year and could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am going to repeat the date and you just wait until I have finished. So the mobilisation of the 216th Brigade in Han Pijesak on the 30th of June 1991, what do you know about that.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that I was present there in my capacity of the president of the Executive Committee of the municipality and the acting chief for national defence. I know that the call up papers were served. According to the planned mobilisation, couriers handed over all the mobilisation papers to the members of that brigade in that military post, and we agreed that they will gather at the football pitch in order to form a battalion as per establishment, and then thereafter to be escorted to Han Pijesak. The president of the municipality and myself remained all the time at the sports centre awaiting the military conscripts. In the local communes where the conscripts resided, we provided for them buses in order to bring them to Rogatica. But something happened and that is the following: Only a handful of Muslims came from these local communes by buses to Rogatica and even fewer of them boarded the buses and headed for the assembly point. The Serbs who received call-up papers, and they accounted for 30 per cent of the strength of the brigade, left to get to the mobilisation point by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us the percentage of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 40 per cent based on the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the record says 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the unit was formed, everybody was called who were there to get on. However, the Muslims refused to leave that area. They did not recognise this army. It was not their army and they did not want to subject themselves to the command of this army. That happened for the first time in the history of organisation up to that point. If you receive call-up papers from the command, you have to respond. The Serbs responded but the Muslims didn't. They remained in Rogatica even though they constituted a majority because 60 per cent, according to the consensus were Muslim inhabitants of Rogatica. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt you for a second. You said when the unit was formed everybody was called who were there to get on. However, the Muslim refused to leave that area. What was the basis for them to be -- for them to have to leave the area. It's not clear to me exactly what you meant by all that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how it was, Mr. President. The brigade in Han Pijesak was meant by the reserve forces of conscripts from Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Olovo, and some of Sarajevo municipalities. The municipality of Rogatica at that time provided about 1200 conscripts from Rogatica for the brigade. Among these 1200 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at that time, what time do you have exactly in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the period up until the 30th of June 1991. In all the preceding years, whenever a mobilisation was carried out everybody would normally respond, both communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please resume where you said the municipality of Rogatica at that time provided about 1200 conscripts for the brigade. And then you said: "Among these 1200 ..." And could you resume from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Among the 1200, 60 per cent were Muslim soldiers and also officers, 40 per cent were Serbian military personnel. As of that day, really nothing was the same as before. The Serbs felt insecure, threatened because their numbers were low anyway and to add to the pressure was the fact that the highest elite members of the SDA, young people, were sent to undergo training in Croatia. Since the Serbian soldiers were mobilised for the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, I'm going to interrupt you because, yeah, I have the feeling that we are not moving in the direction of an answer to my question. The Muslims refused to leave that area. Who required them to leave what area? Who told them you should leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the military drill?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said once the unit was formed everybody was called and so on, however the Muslims refused to leave that area. That is unclear to me what area, who told them that they had to leave, or why would they leave which they refused to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade command invited all the conscripts, regardless of their ethnicity, including the Muslims and Serbs, who came to that point to board the buses and head for Han Pijesak. The SDA party came forward and said that we are not going to go. So people left the files of soldiers and gathered on the sidelines. Some 20 or 30 Muslims did not obey the advice of the SDA. They boarded the buses and they went to the battle-field in Han Pijesak. Two days later the SDA organised a bus service in order to bring them back. They all returned except for two Muslims who remained in the Army of Republika Srpska the whole ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. I still don't think that I've received an answer to what I asked because is it that they had to leave the area where they had gathered or was it -- it's totally unclear to me. But, Mr. Lukic, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with this knowledge could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further explore what I apparently do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where -- just a moment. Where was the gathering point?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gathering point was in Rogatica. All of the soldiers were expected to come there to form a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast. Tell me what happened outside of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly point outside of Rogatica was in Han Pijesak, including the headquarters of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the previous period, was that the assembly point where soldiers who had received these kind of call-up papers were gathering? Go on.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes. Up until 1990, I was a member of that brigade and I had my own war assignment. When I moved to the Executive Committee, I left the brigade and was involved in civilian power. But this assembly mobilisation point was one and the same for all the conscripts and soldiers up until June 1991. So nothing new happened. Everything was according to the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the early period when people who were called up had to leave Rogatica and go to Han Pijesak once they were summoned to join the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Some stayed five days or seven days or fifteen days depending on the exercise, but they reported to the brigade whenever they received call-up papers and there was no problems whatsoever until the 30th of June, 1991, when they were also expected to appear and go to the designated ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this place was where? It was outside was Rogatica in Han Pijesak; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is Rogatica from Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say some 62 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the municipal building of Rogatica, was there any weapons of the TO stocked and guarded?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked there and I know for sure that the municipal building doesn't have any cellar, it only has offices. As for TO weapons, they were kept in the TO building, which has nothing to do with the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the documentation relating to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a participant or at least an observer of all of that to a great extent. Probably after this refusal to respond to a mobilisation and perhaps in fear of being prosecuted for refusing to serve in the army, and at the same time the brigade command wanted to have individual records in its own hands. That's according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak more slowly. The interpreters cannot absolutely catch everything that he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, whatever you say and is omitted is not recorded. Please can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you also already not talking when others are still talking. Take a break. Wait until Mr. Lukic has finished his question, take five seconds, take a breath, and then answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we left off when we said that the brigade command wanted to have these records in their hands, that is according to the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go on from there.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon arrival of two lorries from the Han Pijesak unit, which were parked in front of the building where the TO and the police station shared, the police - particularly Muslim police officers - tried to prevent the taking of these archives. One of the policemen who was in plain clothes saw all this commotion and he came across the park in civilian clothes, the soldier who was providing security, he had a uniform and weapons and I know very well that he had an automatic rifle and a knife at his belt. I personally was watching all this from the window of the municipal building. This rather stocky soldier who was larger than police officer, started choking him. At one point the soldier pulled out the dagger and stabbed him in the abdomen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was recorded that the soldier was bigger than the police officer.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the other way around. His name was, I think, Asim Alagic. So there was chaos, there was mayhem, and quite simply the army did not take the archives because SDA activists and the Muslim police did not allow the archives to be taken away. Only on some of the later occasions after we had agreed on the division we were able to take over the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the nationality of the secretary at the national defence secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This post was allocated to the Muslim side. They chose it. But they did not have a proper candidate to fill this post, so the president of the Executive Committee, by virtue of his office, can fill certain posts that they were vacant with acting officers. That is why I, for a period, discharged the duties of the president of the Executive Committee and the secretary of the national defence, acting secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Starting when did you discharge both these duties?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can say that in fact it was from the 1st of January 1991. The Muslims had three places on the Executive Committee, the Serbs had two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, slow -- slow down. Slow down. You are much too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they had three places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was an agreement that either Muslim or Serb personnel will fill these posts on condition that it was agreed between both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of the TO in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Territorial Defence of Rogatica was the prewar chief of the TO and the commander of the TO, Mr. Mehmed Agic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would kindly ask Mr. Lukic to switch off his microphone when not in use. It would help us understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are invited to switch off the microphone if the witness answers the question because that makes him better understandable by the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, when did the war start in Sarajevo? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either on the 4th or the 6th of April 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew it. I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you manage to maintain peace in Rogatica? Until when?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our desire was to have an ever-lasting peace and we tried hard until sometime around the 21st of May, 1992. It was a painstaking effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the 21st of May 1992, were there any sporadic skirmishes?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not only skirmishes. There were even murders and killings among the Serbian people. On the 6th of May a civilian, Branko Baracek, was killed in Blazevici. On the 21st of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you mention names and dates, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian, Branko Baracek was killed in Blazevici in Borike on the 6th of May. Drazenko Mihajlovic was killed on the 21st of May in Rijs Lazer on the periphery of Rogatica. On the 23rd of May, Bogdan Vukovic, an elderly shepherd, was killed in Zivaljevina. On the 24th of May, again in Borike, from the direction of Zepa, two lads were killed, Rackovic [phoen] and Markovic. Therefore, Muslims started killing randomly here and there to instill unrest among the Serbian people so that they would feel insecure around the entire area of Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the division of Rogatica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my position and function, I was a participant in the negotiating teams for the division of Rogatica, and I was an active participant in the whole process until the end of the division process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the objective of the division?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of the division was as follows: If we couldn't live together, we wanted to live alongside each other without war. We wanted to divide our territory so that Muslim villages would be under Muslim municipal control, whereas Serb villages would be under the authority of the Serbian municipality of Rogatica. It all made sense. It would mean that we would be divided without war, without bloodshed, without any casualties or losses. However, things turned out differently. When the division was finally agreed and when we were split, expert teams drew up division maps and we took those maps to our joint assembly and the joint assembly was made up by both Muslim and Serbs according to the election figures. I have to say that the joint assembly unanimously adopted such a division and that map, and then the assembly of the respective ethnicities confirmed that division at their respective assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4272. [In English] If we can have only one version and enlarged since... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise it. This is a map from the cadastre. It is an overview of Rogatica, a plan of Rogatica depicting streets and neighbourhoods within the town limits. You can see the lines red, green, dotted, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The short lines, there are green and red lines. What do green lines symbolise, what do red line symbolise, those transecting the streets?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green lines represent the barricades of the Muslim ethnicity. There were three, four, five, six, seven, eight, even more of them in the centre of town. And as for the two short red lines, on the right-hand side there is a church across the street and south of that is Zelenovica and Donje Polje. Those were Serb neighbourhoods and there were a barricade there to literally prevent the entry of Muslims into that Serbian neighbourhood. The left-hand side line at the exit out of Rogatica, there is a full line depicting a Serbian neighbourhood and this is also a Serbian barricade. At the same time, it was a check-point for those who were leaving the town or entering it because there were situations when extremists came from Visegrad and from all over the place from the areas which were affected by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please switch off his microphone and could the witness please slow down. It is impossible to interpret accurately. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you do not slow down, we'll just not receive your evidence. You understand that? I mean, the interpreters need to translate your words, otherwise we cannot evaluate this part of the evidence that's before us; that is, what you tell us. Please keep that in mind. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know you don't find it natural to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, again wait for the end of my question. What about the red -- long red lines on the right-hand side of the map, and then on the left-hand side of the screen in the lower part of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full lines, this is before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red line is the separation line before the war started, before the war activities started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we talking about the red line that is almost like a triangle on the right side, the north-eastern side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also ask you the following. You apparently used the expression "separation line before the war started." Was that a kind of an ethnic separation, that's where the Serbs lived and where the Muslims lived, because "separation line" is a term we often use when there is a war; that is, the line which keeps the armed forces apart. Could you tell us what you meant by "separation line before the war"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will find it in my statement. We split the municipality into two parts. That territory within the red line was the territory of the Serbian municipality of Rogatica. That was the part of town which was divided. However, the centre of the town was not as divided and it has never been divided because of the war that started soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that is what was agreed upon in the first -- the early days of May and that the war started, well, let's say around the 20th of May. Is that -- thank you. That clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just come in again. How are we to understand on that line the solid lines and the dotted lines? What do the solid lines indicate and what do the dotted lines mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dotted lines are the lines of separation after the 22nd of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what we do not have on our screen is the second page in English which gives the legend for the lines, green short lines, Muslim roadblocks; red short lines, Serbian roadblocks; and the lower two, separation before 22 of May; and the lowest, that is the double-line, separation line, after the 22nd of May. That's what the legend tells us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I'm interested to know what the dotted line on the right side of the screen means. I think there is no explanation in the legend, inside of the triangle with the solid line. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Gladly. The area within the dotted line, there is a solid line as a barricade of the Serbian people. In that part within the dotted line there is a Serbian Orthodox church and a -- all the houses around the church were Serbian, all to the last. As you go on, there are some mixed households but the area is predominantly inhabited by the Serbian population. The area around the Serbian Orthodox church was predominantly, if not 100 per cent, inhabited by the Serbs living in Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, at page 16, lines 18 and 19, in response to my question, you said: "The dotted lines are the lines of separation after the 22nd of May 1992." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question: The big triangle, you've said it was the separation line before the war, and as I understood you that whole big triangle inside the big red circle was Serb; is that not so? I see you are nodding. So that the record can have your answer, can you say it verbally, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then, now when you say the dotted line inside the circle was the separation line after the 22nd of May, do I understand -- are we still to understand that inside the triangle there was a side where the BiH Army was and there was a side where the Serb army was inside this big red triangle, those parts -- those armies being separated by this dotted line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time we still had Territorial Defence forces. We had a Muslim Territorial Defence and also a Serb Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now I understand that. Whether they were Territorial Defence or whatever they were, are we to understand that inside an area that is enclosed as an exclusively Serb area, Muslims were in there fighting against Serbs and separated by this broken line? Is that how we are to understand this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite the parties to see whether they agree on what it actually means? Because dotted lines, fine. But we have dotted lines single, we have dotted lines together with fixed lines, we have them in red, we have them elsewhere. We have apparently periods where there is no real combat, although murders were committed. It's still pretty unclear to me, but if the parties would have a common understanding on what this map tells us, then I would highly appreciate if they would share their views with the Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, let me just ask you this. On the left-hand side of the screen in its bottom part, there is a solid line and a dotted line. On the left-hand side of that line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Left, north, west, could we seek the assistance of who -- someone who can move a pointer over this picture visible both for the witness and for the Chamber so that when we are talking about lines that we can see on our screen and verify whether we are talking about the same lines yes or no. And I might even have a few questions to further explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then can we use the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps marking --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Marking, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would be better and then make it a new exhibit. Witness, you will be invited to make some markings, but please wait until you have received clear instructions what to mark and how to mark it. So wait before doing anything. Could you draw a line or lines which would depict the division of territory before the 22nd of May 1992. So before the war really started. Could you draw one or more lines and then indicate clearly -- but I'll give you further instructions. Could you tell us what were the separation lines before the 22nd of May and could you draw them, mark them on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This now looks more or less as a -- as an isle within the whole of that territory, a secluded area. Whose territory was that? Was that Serb? Was that Muslim? Could you tell us? First tell us before you start marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Muslims were -- and Serbs were there, more Muslims than the Serbs. This is where the Serbian side was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you not to make any marking. Could the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- assist in erasing the last marking. Okay. Now what I see is a kind of a triangle. Was that a mixed area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put the letter M in the middle of the mixed area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you make it M plus S because otherwise the word M might be misunderstood. So could you make that M plus S, standing for Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there we are. Now, could you draw any other separation line and take it one by one, also before the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you have drawn a line. Could you first answer my question. To the left of that line, who were living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs. This is the Serbian neighbourhood called Karanfil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you add an S to that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what now remains is first what seems to be the centre of town more or less. Who were living there? Was that undivided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That part of the town was not divided. As I said, only where there was a clear majority was subject to division. However, within the town itself there were no divisions and it was actually the war that prevented the division of the centre of the town and the population was of mixed compositions, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that whatever remains now on the map, on which looks as the centre of this map, that that was undivided? Or were there still smaller divisions within that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no minor divisions. Whatever is free of any lines was at the time under the control of the Muslim forces or the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But although under their control, undivided as far as where Serbs lived and where Muslims lived. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then put a letter U in the centre of the area you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, earlier you started to make some marking at the right top part of the map. Could you first tell us what you intended to tell us about that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. To the right of this line in the left corner of the screen, the neighbourhoods were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no -- let me -- let me -- you started marking which was this erased not at the left but at the right top part of the map. So we see more or less three parallel what seems to be roads going to the right top of this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, first of all, that area, who lived there and under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an area mostly populated by Serbs and this part or territory was allocated to the Serb even though there were a few Muslim households. However the roads that lead to Pasic Kula, and to Kozici, and further afield where the barricades were, this is the area where the Muslim villages were. However, you cannot see it on this map because this map depicts only the urban part of the town not rural parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand you well that urban part of town was mainly populated by Serbs but there were some Muslims living there as well? Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The ratio in the town itself was, let's say, 60 per cent, so that the town itself reflected the census; 60 per cent of Muslims and 40 per cent of Serbs. So the ratio within the town itself was almost the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm exclusively talking about the area in the very right upper part of this map. I think you said it was allocated to Serbs even though there were a few Muslim households. Is that true? Could you then put in that area a large S and a very small M?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, in that same answer where you -- where the Judge was asking you about, you further say: "However, the roads that lead to ..." And then we don't know that. "... and then further afield where the barricades were, this is the area where the Muslim villages were." Now, are you -- I'm not quite sure this place that you call "Serbian," is it where the Muslim villages were or are they further afield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, this road in the upper right corner, where you see this green barricade, and further on it leads to Muslim villages, Zlatni Do and Pasic Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be your exhibit? You introduced the map and I think with these clarifications, it would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- still appropriately be a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we would propose this one as our exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number for -- the D number for this map now marked by the witness would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was already D693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The marked version will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked version will be another have exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D693 as marked by the witness receives number D695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D695 is admitted into evidence. And perhaps this is the right moment because earlier I have not expressed the Chamber's decision on admission for D692, D693, and D694. There were no objections. They are now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then D695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 695 was already admitted into evidence. The reason why I delayed it, because you said if the map is explained, and I think it's now thoroughly explained, then you would have no objections. That's the reason why I waited to express our decision until this very moment. Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. How much more time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have some questions left I really have to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But those questions would be quickly answered since it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to ask for too much of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters hope that they will not be too quickly answered. How much time would you need approximately? If you say it's five minutes we might consider, if Mr. Mladic would be agreeable to that, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's more than five minutes. And could I also encourage you to present organised evidence and -- in such a way that the Chamber, which may be a bit slow of understanding, but that we at least understand what is presented before us. We take a break, Witness. You may follow the usher. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would say our apologies for the late start, it would be unfair to my colleagues. My apologies for the late start. Mr. Lukic, could I invite you to do a similar exercise but now for the lines after 22 of May, perhaps in a new map so that we know exactly what it is all about? Perhaps take the same unmarked map now and then draw the lines as they existed on from the 22nd of May. And I know that it takes some time to get the right lines on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I'm hoping for extension of time, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can always try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one difference, Mr. Lukic. I couldn't have done it before court. But we'll be a bit more generous than we usually are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll need the help of the usher again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the usher assist the witness again in marking. Mr. Ujic, please continue at the speed of speech you demonstrated in the last portion of the previous session. Mr. Lukic will now continue. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honours, to speak more slowly, but believe me I can't help it. I am a fast talker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, this map that we have in front of us, can you please indicate the positions of the Muslim and Croat forces -- or rather, I'm sorry, Muslim and Serb forces as well as Muslims and Croats in the town after the 22nd of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll try. May I mark them on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this part of town was held by the Muslim forces because the Serbs had mainly withdrawn from that part of town to the Serbian neighbourhoods to the right and left, and the central part remained under the authority or supervision of the Muslim forces. The Serb forces were here in this part and down here in this part. The 5th Pljesevica, and this was with some elements of forces, was outside of the town, and further on eastwardly towards Borike where the Serbian TO was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the letter M in the middle of this circle and put the letter S in the areas that you marked as Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now what was happening with this red triangle?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red triangle is -- was the place -- or rather the general area was where the war started because there was the body of Drazenko Mihajlovic and the dispute arose because they refused to hand over the body. Then a TO unit on the 22 of May left Borike and took over this part of the territory. And then in the course of war operations where there was some resistance, so in the area marked M plus S, which made use -- also this part of town a military target and it was eventually occupied which altered the situation in the field, combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the help of the usher to erase this M plus S because it was previous situation. So just erase MS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after the 22nd, was this area also in the Serbian hands?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was taken over by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with the S.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is this sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's -- of course, we still have now one circle without any marking and of course for those reading the transcript later on. Do I understand, Witness, that the Serbs took over also the area at the top which is at this moment without any further marking and where you have made an arrow downwards? Then I would suggest, because that's what I now understand, is that we erase that circle and the arrow and that we put a line around what used to be M plus S and now has become S. Mr. Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just erase that circle and arrow -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just erase that circle and arrow at the top part of the screen, as Judge Orie suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And could -- could -- Mr. Lukic, could you instruct the witness to make a circle or draw a line which area was now finally around where the S is was under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, can you please, the S which is outside the circle, can you just place a circle around it to indicate that it was controlled by the Serb? Because the whole triangle is red. Or even wider than that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This whole triangle, I said that where -- that is where the body of the Drazenko Mihajlovic was. So in order for us to pull out his body, we had to occupy this area M plus S which was one of the strongholds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for an explanation as why you did it, but could you please around that S, the triangle, indicate with a circle or triangle, whatever way, which area there was now newly controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D693 as marked by the witness received number D696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D696, that's the second version -- second marked version of D693 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, was there any organised defence in Rogatica conducted by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes. There was fierce defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did the situation persist? I'm referring to the situation depicted on the last map. When did the new fighting start?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime on the 19th of June 1992, low intensity skirmishes started and lasted until the 22nd of July 1992. Then we suppressed the Muslims because they had torched Serbian buildings, houses, apartments, and business premises. We pushed them from the central part denoted by letter M on the map, and that's when the aggression ended. The extremists were separated, the civilians were driven out, and the war stopped there and then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They were not driven out, they were divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serbian units have flamethrowers?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had long been abandoned in the JNA, so there was no grounds for any member of the Serbian forces or any unit of the Serbian forces to have one because they hadn't -- not even existed in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Uzice Corps ever active in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I know a lot, the Uzice Corps never set foot on the territory of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any burnt and charred bodies around Rogatica during the conflict and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see something that didn't exist. They simply did not exist. If they had been there I would have seen them, I suppose. But I really never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In late August 1992, did you see many decomposing bodies in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charred, decomposed? I repeat, never ever did I see them. I didn't see them in June, July, or August, I didn't see a single body, let alone many bodies, either charred or burnt or decomposing. There were none. Or at least I'm not aware of those. In any case, I didn't see any. And I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now something about the departure of civilians from Rogatica. After the conflict, how did people leave Rogatica? I'm referring to civilians. What was the procedure in place?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To -- for the Trial Chamber to understand the situation better, I have to say a few words. From the beginning of the negotiations about the division into two municipalities, many Serb and Muslim families were afraid of what the future might bring. Therefore, both went wherever they could. The Muslim side as a rule took regular buses and got into their cars. Even before the war, a large group went to Sarajevo because most of them had proprieties in Sarajevo. That's where they left with their families. Another large group left in the direction of Gorazde, and the third group withdrew towards Zepa because they hailed from Zepa and they lived in Rogatica. That means that a lot of Muslims had left town even before the first round was fired. A large number of Serb families were also moving to the Serbian neighbourhoods in the south and west of the town or the villages on the periphery of the town. A smaller part of families went to Serbia if they had relatives there. They spent a few months there and then they returned to Rogatica. What I'm saying is that there was no forcible resettlement, really. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about collection centres in Rogatica? Did they exist for civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I already wrote about that. It was like a safe house. Why did I call it a safe house? Because we wanted to separate civilians from those carrying arms. We did not want collateral damage. That's why we separated civilians to the territory under the control of the Serbian army and that was the secondary school Veljko Vlahovic. Another small number were received for a couple of days in the circle surrounded by the dotted red line surrounded -- encircling the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Don't mark anything.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not marking anything. I'm just showing you things. This was not a collection centre but a reception centre for the population from the area marked by a large S. We wanted to accommodate them there because the school was not fit for the purpose. The civilians could have been shot from either one side or the other side, so we would keep them here for a couple of days and then as soon as conditions were in place for their transfer they would be moved to the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the facility where they stayed for a couple of days, what facility was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the church hall or the church house in Rogatica. They were received there, and when there were 10 or 15 of them they would be transferred to the secondary school. If they had been taken to the school one by one, they would have been exposed to a greater danger. That's why we waited for groups of 10 to 15 to be formed. I'll do my best, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put at this moment one question to the witness. You said, Mr. Ujic, that you gave a reason why you separated civilians to the territory under the control of the Serbian army and that was the secondary school Veljko Vlahovic. What ethnicity did these civilians belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all those who did not want to fight because they were not armed, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. It was not just Muslims. They were all civilians who had to be protected from dieing. They were accommodated in that place which was a safe house for them where they could save themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I only asked for their ethnicity. Can you give me a percentage? You said Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. Can you give percentages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't talk percentages. I told you that many had abandoned -- had left the town even before the first round was fire. In any case there were more Muslims because they were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't understand the last word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were also Serbs, there were also Croats. I didn't count heads. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many approximately for each group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I did come to the school on one occasion and I saw my neighbours and my friends and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- certainly there were a lot more Muslims, but I wasn't there when different groups were brought in, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The area around the Veljko Vlahovic school or around Rasadnik, were they mined?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been I would have known. I should have known. However, the school is in the very centre of town, so I really say categorically that it had never occurred to anybody to plant mines around the school. I claim categorically there were no mines planted either around the school or the Rasadnik. We did not have them. Even if we had wanted to plant them, we did not have them at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the short answer would have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to my knowledge, no. That's all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only thing that wasn't recorded was that the school was in the territory controlled under the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The school was in the territory controlled by the Serbs then and now, still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What food was given to the people who were accommodated in the Veljko Vlahovic school? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have personal knowledge of that. I saw that the food came from the same place for the troops on the line, for the refugees in Rogatica and for those who were in the Veljko Vlahovic school and later on in Rasadnik. That means that they received three meals a day and the same meals were served to all the three categories of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think that's already in the statement, isn't it? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what was the attitude of Muslim fighters to the people who remained living in Muslim villages or in Rogatica, those who were of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. Muslim fighters considered those people traitors because they had stayed with Chetniks. They were their relatives' neighbours. They held it against them for having stayed in the Serb-controlled territory. There were even attempts by Muslims to murder or to kill their fellow nationals for having stayed in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the entire villages remain populated by the Muslim population after the conflict broke out and then until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that that was the case, and I'm talking about Satorovici, Okruglo, Tmorni Do, and Osovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing was recorded. Slowly one name after the next.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages are Satorovici, Okruglo, Okruglo. Now it has been recorded twice. Tmorni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tmorni Do. And finally the village of Osovo. And another one, Burati.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the inhabitants of those villages who had handed over weapons and did not want to seek protection in those collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who had handed over were weapons and didn't want to go to collection centres, who wanted to stay in their houses, did stay there. For example, in Satorovic there was a retired JNA General Asim Hodzic with his wife. He stayed there with his fellow villagers. He rallied them and he acted as their advisors -- advisor as to what to do. He advised them to respect the authorities of the territory where they lived. They all received food from the Crisis Staff and they received the same quantity per capita as a person of Serb ethnicity. So a Muslim received as much oil, wheat, flour, coffee, detergent as a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now just briefly, I would like to ask you something about the destruction of religious facilities in Rogatica. Was a mosque destroyed in Rogatica in June?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As you look at the plan, you will see the territory controlled by Muslims. The two mosques were there. I heard that the mosque had been destroyed. And later, a couple of days later, there was an explosion, an anti-tank mine had been planted under the ruins of the mosque and our APC, which was driving from north to south, hit the mine, a soldier was killed, he was driving the APC, and the other was wounded, seriously wounded. I only know that from that mosque --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question asked was whether a mosque was destroyed. You are giving us long explanations as to who may have done it or may not have done it. Although the -- you started your answer by "I don't know." Was there a mosque destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I don't know the date when that happened, but I know that a mosque had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's what happens if you put a composite question, Mr. Lukic. So you know a mosque was destroyed. You don't know whether it happened in June. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it that you don't know the date or you don't know at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I am sure it was in June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the simple answer would have been: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, at the time when the mosque was destroyed was that part of town under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they were not even close. And you can see that in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the synagogue?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we entered the town on the 23rd of July and we pushed the Muslims from the central circle M, this is where the synagogue was, we found the synagogue razed to the ground and burned. That was the only Jewish religious building. Prior to that it was a cultural centre where exhibitions were held but now it was demolished and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the Catholic church? Has it remained until the end of war?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Catholic church? Yes. It's here in the Serb controlled territory and it remained totally intact. There is not even a bullet-hole in it. It is still there standing as it had been standing before and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now something completely different. Do you know when Tomo Batinic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of the municipality. I think that that happened sometime in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have two or three questions and then we'll round it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you asked for an hour, you asked for additional time for my invitation to have some additional markings. I said I would be generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need two more minutes or one more minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine because you -- all together you took already quite a bit more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, have you ever been informed about a plan to kill one-third of Muslims in Rogatica, to convert one-third into Christianity, and one-third to be expelled?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility before this Court that such a plan never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the last statement, that you never heard of it, is fully acceptable. That it did not exist would suggest that you could look into the minds of everyone, which of course you cannot. So we do understand that you never heard of such a plan. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself carry out something like that on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen anyone else doing that during the war in Rogatica on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything like that and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you'll be cross-examined by the Prosecution, I have one clarifying question. You marked those maps. Did I understand you well that the Muslim control over the centre of the town, as you marked it, that that lasted until, well, let's say, 23rd of July I think you said, and that after that Serbs had taken over control also over the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you described in some detail about Serbs being killed early May, I think the last incident you mentioned was the 24th, you gave names, et cetera. During that period of time, were only some Serbs murdered or were there also killings committed against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, believe me, as much as I would like to tell the truth I knew about those Serb victims because that was in our territory. As for the losses in the Muslim territory, that's something that I wasn't able to see; therefore, I wouldn't like to say anything. Even if there was a single victim, it's a victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a clear answer. My last question would be about the Vlahovic secondary school. You emphasized very much that people were taken there in order to protect them against any violence. My first question is did you hear of anyone being taken there not on his own free will but because he was forced to go to that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about somebody being forced, but I remember one specific situation. Once we decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you whether you are aware of anyone, and let's limit ourselves to Muslims, that had gone to that school not of their own free will but because they were compelled to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. Anyone who didn't want to leave, just like the people from Satorovici village, stayed behind because there were no war operations. Only the Muslims from the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why not answer my question directly. Are you aware of anyone who didn't go there of his own free will but was compelled by others to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's my answer. If they were called through the megaphone for civilians to be separated, that would maybe be a kind of force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please resume from where you said: "... that may be a kind of force ..." Could you resume from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said if they were called on a megaphone by the then president of the TO to be separated from people under arms and to go to the secondary school, if you consider that force, then that's how it happened. Nobody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- else came under duress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You say if they were called on a megaphone, did it happen that people were called on a megaphone to go to the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain this further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Witness, just tell me whether people were called through a megaphone to go to the Vlahovic secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but only once when the centre of town was at stake it was necessary to separate the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it was a necessity or not is another matter. So therefore people were called and told that they had to go to the Vlahovic school; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whoever wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did they say? If you want to go to the school, please do so, or did they say you have to go to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were invited in order to save their lives to go to the school because there was an impending war operation in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say that if they wouldn't go to the school that their life was at stake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the supposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You emphasized very much how people were going there to be protected. Was that protection effective in that everyone could later on leave the school sound and safe and go to wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Your Honours, when a certain number would assemble, they had families elsewhere and they wanted to reunite with their families. I know very well that they were issued papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That's the second part of my question, whether they could go wherever they wanted to go. But was everyone sound and safe when leaving the school? Did everyone survive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you mean. I heard, even though the intention was for everyone who goes to the school that their lives would be guaranteed; however, I heard that some 25 people were to be transferred from the school to Rasadnik and they ended the way they ended. I find it appalling, I don't know what kind of pervert and insane person can do that. I still don't understand it. However, those who survived at the school, if they said that they would like to travel, we gave them paper to list members of their families, we provided police escort for them as far as the separation line, and then we would hand them over safe and sound. But I know that according to the list some wanted to go to Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, Skopje, or east or western European countries. So within the limitations that we had we accommodated their request and they reunited with their families safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Do you have any -- were you present when these persons were given a free choice where they would wish to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't. But I was told that that was how it was done by the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Now finally you said they ended as they ended and you couldn't understand how an any sane person could apparently do -- do I take that as a reference to them being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any personal knowledge about how they were killed? Under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you what I know. At the time I was at the head of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked for personal knowledge. Let that be clear. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no personal knowledge, but I have intelligence report that arrived quite soon after the event. I don't know whether it was on the same day or the next day. I received information that something like that had happened. I couldn't believe that even then, just as I cannot believe it to this date. Even though I was a defence witness for this executioner in the BH court, I still cannot believe that such a mind, disturbed mind, can do something like that without being given any order to that effect, an individual. I found it totally incomprehensible and today I find it totally illogical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you concluded that the person who committed killings must have acted under orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That should have been the case, but apparently this person did not act in that manner because I can claim with full responsibility that nobody issued this kind of order ever. I can confirm that categorically. He did it on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you tell us that you are not aware of anyone who would have given such an order. Is that a right understanding of your claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it so that these people were killed by one individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there on the spot, but according to the judgement and the trial, probably the prosecutors office investigated the whole case and found out who the perpetrator was. That's why he was put on trial. And everybody is convinced through the evidence and documents in the case filed that he was the culprit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I asked the question because of the answer that you gave at page 44, lines 14 to 22. Right through that you talk of individual. "I couldn't believe that even then, just as I cannot believe it now to date, even though I was a defence witness for this executioner in the BH court, I still cannot without being given any order to that effect an individual ..." I don't know what that sentence is. But you mentioned "individual," you mentioned "executioner." That's why I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, just to be sure, are you telling us that there was only one person who committed the killing and that he was not joined by others and that others participated in the -- in what happened, that he was one single individual? Or don't you know? If you don't know, then tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really wish, and I am fully aware of the declaration that I made to tell you the truth, I cannot say with full responsibility whether he had any accomplices or not. But according to the judgement, I understand that he was the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi you'll find him to your right. You're looking at him already. He speaks almost as slow as Mr. Lukic does, so would you please follow his example. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will endeavour uncharacteristically, I'm afraid, to set a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I have a couple of very brief questions to follow-up on the questions the Chamber just asked you. First, you testified that people were called on a megaphone to go to the Vlahovic school by the commander of the Territorial Defence at the time. My question is simply that man was Rajko Kusic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, how many times were you at the school yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there to the school only once. When a large group of people or residents were called on a megaphone in the square where I lived, and there were also some neighbours of mine. I wanted to go and see those people. I took cigarettes, gave them. I spoke to them kindly. I told them, "Don't worry, once this is over you will be back in your homes and in your work-place and you will continue as you did before the war." But it seems that something happened and it seems that not all of them were able to return. But at the time when I went, there were no complaints about the clothing, the food, et cetera. What was happening later on, I don't know. There were some rumours, there were some foolish things that would be done, and somebody said, "Don't interfere with this because it seems that a human life is cheaper than a piece of food."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
